ثم إن ملك الغربان قال لذلك الغراب: كيف صبرت على صحبة البوم ولا صبر للأخيار على صحبة الأشرار؟ قال الغراب: إن ما قلته أيها الملك لكذلك، فإنه يقال لذع النار أيسر على المرء من صحبة الأشرار والإقامة معهم، ولكن العاقل إذا أتاه الأمر الفظيع الذي يخاف من عدم تحمُّله الجائحة على نفسه وقومه لم يجزع من شدَّة الصبر عليه لما يرجو من أن يعقبه صبره حسن العاقبة وكثير الخير، فلم يجد لذلك ألمًا ولم تكره نفسه الخضوع لمَنْ هو دونه حتى يبلغ حاجته فيغتبط بخاتمة أمره وعاقبة صبره.

فقال الملك: أخبرني عن عقول البوم. قال الغراب: لم أجد فيهنَّ عاقلاً إلاَّ الذي كان يحثُّهنَّ على قتلي وكان حرَّضهنَّ على ذلك مرارًا فكنَّ أضعف شيء رأيًا فلم ينظرن في أمري ويذكرن أني قد كنت ذا منزلة في الغربان وأني أُعدُّ من ذوي الرأي ولم يتخوَّفن مكري وحيلتي ولا قبلن من الناصح الشفيق ولا أخفين دوني أسرارهن وقد قالت العلماء: ينبغي للملك أن يحصِّن أموره من أهل النَّميمة ولا يطلع أحدًا منهم على مواضع سرِّه. وقد قيل: ينبغي للمرء أن يتحفَّظ من عدوه في كل شيء حتى في الماء الذي يشربه ويغتسل به، والفراش الذي ينام عليه، والحلة التي يلبسها. والدابة التي يركبها، ولا يأمن على نفسه إلاَّ الثقة الأمين السالم الباطن والظاهر ويكون بعد ذلك كله على حذر منه؛ لأن عدوَّه لا يتوصَّل إليه إلاَّ من جهة ثقاته، فربما كان أحدهم لعدوِّه صديقًا فيصل العدو إلى مراده منه.

فقال الملك: ما أهلك البوم في نفسي إلاَّ البغي وضعف رأي الملك وموافقته وزراء السوء فقال الغراب: صدقت أيها الملك، إنه قلَّما ظفر أحد ولم يطغَ، وقلَّما حرص الرجل على النساء ولم يفتضح، وقلَّ مَنْ أكثر من الطعام ولم يمرض، وقلَّ مَنْ وثق بوزراء السوء وسلم من أن يقع في المهالك، وكان يقال: لا يطمعن ذو الكبر في حسن الثناء، ولا الخبُّ في حسن الصديق، ولا السيئ الآداب في الشرف، ولا الشحيح في البرِّ، ولا الحريص في قلَّة الذنوب، ولا الملك المختال المتهاون بالأمور الضعيف الوزراء في ثبات ملكه وصلاح رعيته.

قال الملك: لقد احتملت مشقَّة شديدة في تصنُّعك للبوم وتضرُّعك إليهن. قال الغراب: إنه مَنْ احتمل مشقَّة يرجو نفعها ونحى نفسه الأنفة والحمية ووطَّنها على الصبر حمد غبَّ رأيه. وإنه يقال: لو أن رجلاً حمل عدوَّه على عنقه وهو يرجو هلاكه وراحته منه لكان ذلك عنده خفيفًا كما صبر الأسود على حمل ملك الضفادع على ظهره وشبع بذلك وعاش. قال الملك: وكيف كان ذلك؟

قال الغراب: زعموا أن أسود من الحيَّات كبر وضعف بصره وذهبت قوته فلم يستطع صيدًا ولم يقدر على طعام. وإنه انساب يلتمس شيئًا يعيش به حتى انتهى إلى عين كثيرة الضفادع قد كان يأتيها قبل ذلك فيصيب من ضفادعها رزقه. فرمى نفسه قريبًا منهنَّ مظهرًا للكآبة والحزن. فقال له أحدها: ما لي أراك أيها الأسود كئيبًا حزينًا؟ قال: ومَنْ أحرى بطول الحزن مني؟ وإنما كان أكثر معيشتي مما كنت أصيب من الضفادع فابتليت ببلاء حرمت عليَّ الضفادع من أجله حتى إني إذا التقيت ببعضها لا أقدر على إمساكه.

فانطلق الضفدع إلى ملك الضفادع فبشَّره بما سمع من الأسود؛ فأتى ملك الضفادع إلى الأسود فقال له: كيف كان أمرك؟ قال: سعيت منذ أيام في طلب ضفدع وذلك عند المساء فاضطررته إلى بيت ناسك ودخلت في أثره في الظلمة، وفي البيت ابن للنَّاسك. فأصبت إصبعه فظننت أنها الضفدع فلدغته فمات؛ فخرجت هاربًا فتبعني النَّاسك في أثري ودعا عليَّ ولعنني وقال: كما قتلت ابني البريء ظلمًا وتعديًا أدعو عليك أن تذلَّ وتصير مركبًا لملك الضفادع فلا تستطيع أخذها ولا أكل شيء منها إلاَّ ما يتصدَّق به عليك ملكها؛ فأتيت إليك لتركبني مُقرًا بذلك راضيًا به.

فرغب ملك الضفادع في ركوب الأسود وظنَّ أن ذلك فخر له وشرف ورفعة فركبه واستطاب ذلك. فقال له الأسود: قد علمت أيها الملك أني محروم فاجعل لي رزقًا أعيش به. قال ملك الضفادع: لعمري لا بد من رزق يقوم بك إذا كنت مركبي فأمر له بضفدعين يؤخذان في كل يوم ويدفعان إليه؛ فعاش بذلك ولم يضرَّه خضوعه للعدوِّ الذليل بل انتفع بذلك وصار له رزقًا ومعيشة.

وكذلك كان صبري على ما صبرت عليه التماسًا لهذا النفع العظيم الذي اجتمع لنا فيه الأمن والظفر وهلاك العدوِّ والراحة منه. ووجدت صرعة اللين والرِّفق أسرع وأشدُّ استئصالاً للعدوِّ من صرعة المكابرة والعناد، فإن النار لا تزيد بحدَّتها وحرِّها إذا أصابت الشجرة على أن تحرق ما فوق الأرض منها، والماء بلينه وبرده يستأصل ما تحت الأرض منها، ويقال: أربعة أشياء لا يستقلُّ قليلها: النار والمرض والعدو والدِّين.

قال الغراب: وكل ذلك كان من رأي الملك وأدبه وسعادة جدِّه. وإنه كان يقال: إذا طلب اثنان أمرًا ظفر به منهما أفضلهما مروءة، فإن اعتدلا في المروءة فأشدُّهما عزمًا، فإن استويا في العزم فأسعدهما جدًا. وكان يقال: مَنْ حارب الملك الحازم الأريب المتضرِّع الذي لا تبطره السرَّاء ولا تدهشه الضرَّاء كان هو داعي الحتف إلى نفسه. ولاسيما إذا كان مثلك أيها الملك العالم بفروض الأعمال ومواضع الشدَّة واللين والغضب والرضا والمعاجلة والأناة الناظر في أمر يومه وغده وعواقب أعماله.

قال الملك للغراب: بل برأيك وعقلك ونصيحتك ويمن طالعك كان ذلك. فإن رأي الرجل الواحد العاقل الحازم أبلغ في هلاك العدوِّ من الجنود الكثيرة من ذوي البأس والنجدة والعدد والعدَّة، وإن من عجيب أمرك عندي طول لبثك بين ظهراني البوم تسمع الكلام الغليظ ثمَّ لم تسقط بينهن بكلمة.
قال الغراب: لم أزل متمسكا بأدبك أيها الملك أصحب البعيد والقريب بالرِّفق واللين والمبالغة والمؤاتاة

قال الملك: أصبحت وقد وجدتك صاحب العمل ووجدت غيرك من الوزراء أصحاب أقاويل ليس لها عاقبة حميدة، فقد منَّ الله علينا بك منَّة عظيمة لم نكن قبلها نجد لذَّة الطعام والشراب ولا النوم ولا القرار، وكان يقال: لا يجد المريض لذَّة الطعام والنوم حتى يبرأ، ولا الرجل الشَّره الذي قد أطمعه سلطانه في مال وعمل في يده حتى ينجزه له، ولا الرجل الذي قد ألحَّ عليه عدوُّه وهو يخافه صباحًا ومساءً حتى يستريح منه قلبه، ومَنْ وضع الحمل الثقيل عن يده أراح نفسه، ومَنْ أمن عدوَّه ثلج صدره.

قال الغراب: أسأل الله الذي أهلك عدوك أن يمتِّعك بسلطانك، وأن يجعل في ذلك صلاح رعيتك ويشركهم في قرَّة العين بملكك، فإن الملك إذا لم يكن في ملكه قرَّة عيون رعيته فمثله مثل زنمة العنز التي يمصُّها الجدي وهو يحسبها حلمة الضرع فلا يصادف فيها خيرًا.
قال الملك: أيها الوزير الصالح كيف كانت سيرة البوم وملكها في حروبها وفيما كانت فيه من أمورها؟

قال الغراب: كانت سيرته سيرة بطر وأشر وخيلاء وعجز وفخر مع ما فيه من الصفات الذميمة، وكل أصحابه ووزرائه شبيه به إلاَّ الوزير الذي كان يشير عليه بقتلي فإنه كان حكيمًا أريبًا فيلسوفًا حازمًا قلَّما يُرَى مثله في علو الهمة وكمال العقل وجودة الرأي.

قال الملك: وأي خصلة كانت أدلُّ على عقله. قال: خلَّتان إحداهما رأيه في قتلي، والأخرى أنه لم يكن يكتم صاحبه نصيحته وإن استقلَّها، ولم يكن كلامه كلام عنف وقسوة ولكنه كلام رفق ولين حتى إنه ربما أخبره ببعض عيوبه ولا يصرِّح بحقيقة الحال بل يضرب له الأمثال ويحدثه بعيب غيره فيعرف عيبه فلا يجد ملكه إلى الغضب عليه سبيلاً، وكان مما سمعته يقول لملكه أنه قال: لا ينبغي للملك أن يغفل عن أمره فإنه أمر جسيم لا يظفر به من الناس إلاَّ قليل ولا يدرك إلاَّ بالحزم، فإن المُلْكَ عزيز فمَنْ ظفر به فليحسن حفظه وتحصينه، فإنه قد قيل إنه في قلَّة بقائه بمنزلة قلَّة بقاء الظلِّ عن ورق النيلوفر. وهو في خفة زواله وسرعة إقباله وإدباره كالرِّيح، وفي قلة ثباته كاللبيب مع اللئام، وفي سرعة اضمحلاله كحباب الماء من وقع المطر.
فهذا مثل أهل العداوة الذين لا ينبغي أن يغترَّ بهم وإن هم أظهروا تودُّدًا وتضرُّعًا.

english.text: The Owls and the Crows

King Dabshalim said to Bidpai the philosopher: "I have heard the example of loyal friends and their cooperation. Now give me an example of an enemy whom one must not trust, even when he displays humility and flattery." The philosopher said: "Whoever is deceived by an enemy who has always been an enemy will suffer what the owls suffered from the crows." The king asked: "How was that?"

Bidpai said: "They relate that on a mountain stood a great spreading tree in which a thousand crows nested, ruled by one of their own number. Near this tree was a cave containing a thousand owls, also ruled by one of their number. The king of the owls went out on one of his excursions, harboring enmity toward the king of the crows; the crows and their king felt the same toward the owls. The owl king and his followers raided the crows in their nests, killing and capturing many. The attack took place at night.

"In the morning the crows gathered before their king and said: 'You know what we suffered last night from the owl king. Not one of us escaped being killed, wounded, having a wing broken, feathers plucked, or a tail torn off. More harmful than the injuries we suffered is their boldness against us and their knowledge of our dwelling. They will return and never leave us alone, now that they know where we are. We are yours, and the decision is yours, O king. Consider our welfare and your own.'

"Among the crows were five recognized for sound judgment, upon whom important matters were laid and to whom the reins of affairs were entrusted. The king often consulted them and took their advice concerning events and calamities. He said to the first: 'What is your opinion in this matter?' The crow said: 'An opinion in which the learned have preceded us: they have said that against an enraged enemy there is nothing but flight.' The king asked the second for his opinion. He answered: 'My opinion is the same as his: flight.'

"The king said: 'I do not consider it sound advice to leave our homeland and abandon it to our enemy after the first reverse he has inflicted on us. We should not do that. Rather, we should gather our strength, prepare against our enemy, kindle the fire of war between us, and guard against surprise when he approaches. We should meet him ready and fight without retreat or negligence. Our outposts should confront his, while we safeguard ourselves in our strongholds. We should repel him sometimes with patience and sometimes with hard fighting, wherever we find our opportunity and objective, until we have turned him away.'

"Then the king asked the third: 'What do you think?' He said: 'I do not consider what those two said sound advice. We should send out watchers, dispatch spies, and station scouts between ourselves and our enemy, to discover whether he wants peace, war, or tribute. If we find him coveting wealth, we should not reject peace in return for an annual payment that protects us and lets us live securely in our country. It is among the policies of kings, when their enemy's strength becomes formidable and they fear for themselves and their lands, to make wealth a shield for the country, the kingship, and the subjects.'

"The king asked the fourth: 'What do you think of this peace?' He answered: 'I do not consider it sound. Better to leave our homeland and endure exile and hardship than to throw away our honor and submit to an enemy less noble than ourselves. Besides, if we offered this to the owls, they would be satisfied with nothing short of excessive demands. It is said in proverbs: Draw somewhat nearer to your enemy to gain your object, but do not draw entirely near, lest he grow bold against you, your troops weaken, and you abase yourself. This is like a stick set up in the sunshine. If you incline it a little, its shadow grows; if you incline it beyond the proper limit, the shadow shrinks. Our enemy will not be content with a modest concession. The policy for us and for you is war.'

"The king asked the fifth: 'What do you say? Which do you advise: fighting, peace, or departure from our homeland?' He answered: 'As for fighting, a person has no business fighting someone he cannot overcome. It is said that whoever does not know himself and his enemy, and fights someone beyond his strength, brings death upon himself. Moreover, the wise do not belittle an enemy. Whoever belittles his enemy is deceived about him, and whoever is deceived about his enemy does not escape him unharmed. I greatly fear the owls, even if they desist from fighting us. I feared them before this, for the prudent are never secure against an enemy in any condition. If he is distant, they do not feel safe from his assault; if close, from his sudden leap; if alone, from his cunning.

"'The most prudent and intelligent are those who dislike fighting because of its cost. Measures short of battle cost money, words, and effort; battle costs lives and bodies. Let fighting the owls therefore not be your policy, O king, for whoever fights an adversary beyond his strength hazards his own life. When a king protects his secrets, carefully chooses his ministers, commands awe in people's eyes, and is difficult to overpower, he is unlikely to be stripped of the sound advantages he has received. You, O king, are such a ruler. You have consulted me about a matter to which my answer is partly public and partly secret. Secrets have different ranks: some may be shared with a group, some require the assistance of a company, and some admit only two people. Given the importance of this secret, I think only four ears and two tongues should share it.'

"The king rose at once, withdrew privately with him, and sought his counsel. His first question was: 'Is the origin of the hostility between us and the owls known?' The crow answered: 'Yes. It began with a word spoken by a crow.' The king asked: 'How was that?'

"The crow said: 'They relate that a company of cranes had no king and agreed to make the owl king their ruler. While they were assembled, a crow alighted nearby. They said: "If this crow came to us, we would consult him." Before long he came, and they asked his advice. He said: "Even if birds disappeared from every region, and peacocks, ducks, ostriches, and doves vanished from the world, you would not be compelled to make owls your rulers. They are the ugliest birds to look at, the worst in character, the least intelligent, the fiercest in anger, and the farthest from mercy, besides their blindness and poor sight by day. Worse and uglier still are their foolishness and bad conduct. Unless, of course, you intend to appoint them while managing affairs yourselves with your own judgment and intelligence, as the hare did who claimed the moon was her king, then acted according to her own judgment." The birds asked: "How was that?"'"

The crow said: "They relate that successive years of drought struck a land inhabited by elephants. It became barren; water dwindled, springs sank, plants withered, and trees dried up. The elephants suffered great thirst and complained to their king. He sent messengers and scouts in every direction to seek water. One returned and reported: 'At such-and-such a place I have found a spring called the Moon's Spring, with abundant water.' The elephant king went there with his followers so that he and his elephants might drink. The spring lay in a country of hares. The elephants trampled the hares in their burrows and killed many of them.

"The hares gathered before their king and said: 'You know what the elephants have done to us.' He said: 'Let every one of you who has a plan present it.' A hare called Fayruz came forward. The king knew her for good judgment and refinement. She said: 'If the king thinks fit, let him send me to the elephants with a trustworthy companion who can see and hear what I say and report it to him.' The king answered: 'You are trustworthy, and we accept your word. Go to the elephants and deliver whatever message you wish on my behalf. Know that an envoy's judgment, intelligence, gentleness, and merit reveal the intelligence of the sender. Be gentle, gracious, forbearing, and deliberate. An envoy softens hearts by kindness and hardens them by roughness.'

"The hare set out on a moonlit night and reached the elephants. She did not want to go close to them, fearing they might tread on her and kill her unintentionally. She climbed to a high place on the mountain and called to the elephant king: 'The moon has sent me to you. A messenger is not to blame for the message he delivers, even if he speaks harshly.' The elephant king asked: 'What is the message?' She said: 'He says to you: Whoever knows his superior strength over the weak and is thereby deceived into dealing with the strong as though they were weak will find his strength a disaster. You have learned your superior power over other creatures and been deceived by it. You deliberately came to the spring named after me, drank from it, and muddied it. He has sent me to warn you not to do this again. If you do, I shall darken your sight and destroy your life. If you doubt my message, come to the spring at once, and I shall meet you there.'

"The elephant king was astonished at the hare's words and went to the spring with Fayruz the envoy. When he looked into it, he saw the moonlight there. Fayruz said: 'Take water with your trunk, wash your face with it, and bow down before the moon.' The elephant put his trunk in the water, stirring it, and imagined that the moon trembled. He asked: 'Why has the moon trembled? Do you think he is angry because I put my trunk into the water?' Fayruz answered: 'Yes.' The elephant bowed to the moon again, repented of what he had done, and promised that neither he nor any of his elephants would repeat it."

The crow said: "Besides everything I have told you about the owls, they possess guile, cunning, and deceit. The worst ruler is a deceiver. Whoever is afflicted by a deceiver's tongue and serves him will suffer what befell the hare and the partridge when they submitted their dispute to the cat." The cranes asked: "How was that?"

The crow said: "I had a partridge neighbor at the foot of a tree near my nest, and he often visited me. Then I missed him. I did not know where he had gone, and his absence grew long. A hare came and inhabited the partridge's dwelling. I disliked quarreling with the hare, so she lived there for some time. Eventually the partridge returned and found the hare in his home. He said: 'This place belongs to me. Leave it.' The hare answered: 'The dwelling is mine and in my possession. You are the claimant. If you have a right, prepare to prove it against me.'

"The partridge said: 'There is a judge near us. Come to him with me.' The hare asked: 'Who is the judge?' He answered: 'On the seashore there is a devout cat who fasts by day and prays all night. He harms no creature and sheds no blood. He lives on grass and what the sea casts up for him. If you wish, we can submit to his judgment and accept it.' The hare said: 'I shall be very happy with him if he is as you describe.' They set off, and I followed to see the judgment of this fasting, prayerful creature.

"When the cat saw the hare and partridge approaching, he stood up to pray, displaying humility and devotion. They marveled at his condition, drew near in awe, greeted him, and asked him to judge between them. He told them to relate their story, and they did. He said: 'Old age has overtaken me, and my hearing is weak. Come closer and let me hear what you say.' They approached, repeated their story, and asked for judgment.

"He said: 'I understand what you have told me. Before judging between you, I shall begin with advice. I command you to fear God and seek only the truth. The seeker of truth succeeds even when judgment goes against him; the seeker of falsehood is defeated even when judgment is given in his favor. A person has nothing of this world that is truly his, neither money nor friend, except the righteous deeds he sends ahead. The intelligent should devote their efforts to seeking what endures and will benefit them tomorrow, and should reject efforts spent upon other worldly things. To the wise, money has the standing of a clod of earth. In wishing people good and wishing evil kept from them, he regards them as he regards himself.'

"The cat continued addressing them with such words until they trusted him, turned toward him, and came close. Then he sprang upon them and killed them."

The crow said: "Along with the ill fortune I have described, owls combine every other fault. Do not consider making them your rulers." When the cranes heard the crow's words, they abandoned the plan to choose the owls. An owl present had heard what they said. He told the crow: "You have done me the greatest injury, and I know of no previous wrong I did you that required this. Know that a tree cut by an axe grows again, and flesh cut by a sword heals again; but the tongue's wound does not heal, and what it severs cannot be mended. An arrowhead enters the flesh and is then drawn out; words like arrowheads, once they reach the heart, are neither removed nor extracted. Every fire has something to extinguish it: water for fire, medicine for poison, patience for sorrow. But the fire of hatred never dies. You crows have planted between us and yourselves the tree of resentment, enmity, and hatred."

When the owl finished speaking, he went away angrily and told the owl king what had happened and everything the crow had said. The crow then regretted his rashness and said: "By God, how foolishly I spoke, bringing enmity and hatred upon myself and my people! If only I had not described this situation to the cranes or informed them of this matter! Perhaps most birds have seen more than I have and know many times what I know, but refrained from speaking as I did because they guarded against what I failed to guard against and considered consequences I neglected. This is especially true of the most dreadful kind of speech, whose hearer and speaker both suffer harm from the resentment and malice it creates. Such things should not be called words, but arrows.

"Even when the wise are confident of their strength and merit, they should not let this lead them to bring enmity upon themselves in reliance on their judgment and power, just as one who possesses an antidote should not drink poison in reliance on it. The merit of a person whose actions are good, even if his speech fails him at the outset, becomes clear in the outcome and in the test. The fine speaker, though people admire his skillful descriptions of affairs, may reach no praiseworthy end. I am a speaker whose words will have no good outcome. Was it not foolish of me to venture to speak on a grave matter without consulting anyone or applying considered judgment? Whoever does not consult loyal advisers and acts on his own opinion without repeated examination and reflection will not be pleased with where his judgment leads. How little need I had of what I have gained today, and the anxiety into which I have fallen!"

The crow reproached himself with these and similar words, then departed. "That," said the adviser, "is what you asked about the beginning of the enmity between us and the owls. As for fighting, you know my opinion and my aversion to it. But I have a plan and a stratagem other than fighting that may bring relief, if God Most High wills. Many have used their judgment to devise a way to obtain what they sought. One example is the group who prevailed over the ascetic and took his young goat." The king asked: "How was that?"

The crow said: "They relate that an ascetic bought a large young goat to offer as a sacrifice and led it away. Some tricksters saw him and agreed to take it from him. One accosted him and said: 'Ascetic, what is this dog you have with you?' Another met him and said to a companion: 'This is no ascetic, for an ascetic does not lead a dog.' They kept saying this and similar things until the ascetic no longer doubted that what he was leading was a dog and that the seller had bewitched his eyes. He let it go, and the schemers took it and went away.

"I give you this example because I hope we may attain our object by gentle means and stratagem. I want the king to peck me before witnesses, pluck my feathers and tail, and throw me at the foot of this tree. Then let the king and his troops move to such-and-such a place. I hope to endure, discover the owls' circumstances, the positions of their defenses and entrances, deceive them, and return to you so that we may attack them and gain our purpose against them, if God Most High wills."

The king asked: "Will you submit to that willingly?" The crow answered: "Yes. How should I not, when it promises the greatest relief for the king and his troops?" The king did to the crow what he had requested and then departed. The crow began groaning and murmuring until the owls saw him and heard his groans. They informed their king, who approached to question him about the crows. When he drew near, he ordered an owl to question him. The owl asked: "Who are you, and where are the crows?" He said: "My name is such-and-such. As for what you ask me, I suppose you can see that I am in no condition to know their secrets."

The owl king was told: "This is the crow king's minister and counselor. Let us ask what offense caused him to be treated like this." The crow was questioned and answered: "Our king consulted our company about you. I was present when he said: 'Crows, what do you advise?' I replied: 'O king, we cannot withstand the owls in battle, for they strike harder and are more courageous than we. I advise seeking peace and offering tribute for it. If the owls accept, well and good; otherwise we should flee through the lands. Fighting between us and the owls would benefit them and harm us. Peace is better than strife.' I urged them to abandon war and gave examples to support this. I told them that nothing averts the violence and wrath of a powerful enemy like submission. Do you not see how grass survives a violent wind through its softness and by bending wherever the wind blows?

"But they disobeyed me, declared that they wanted battle, and suspected my words. They said: 'You have joined the owls against us.' They rejected my advice and counsel, tortured me as you see, and the king and his troops left me and departed. I have known nothing of them since."

When the owl king heard the crow's account, he asked one of his ministers: "What do you say about this crow? What do you advise?" The minister said: "I advise nothing but killing him at once. He is the crows' greatest resource. Killing him will relieve us of his cunning, and his loss will weigh heavily upon the crows. It is said: Whoever finds the moment when a task can succeed but does not promptly do what it requires is not wise. Whoever seeks a great objective, is given the opportunity, and neglects it loses the matter, and the chance may never return. Whoever finds his enemy weak and fails to kill him regrets it when the enemy grows strong and is beyond his power."

The king asked another minister: "What do you think of this crow?" He answered: "I advise against killing him. A humbled enemy with no defender deserves to be spared, shown mercy, and forgiven, especially one seeking refuge in fear, who deserves protection."

The owl king asked another of his ministers: "What do you say about the crow?" He replied: "I advise sparing him and treating him kindly, for he is likely to give you faithful counsel. The wise regard hostility among their enemies as a welcome victory, and their enemies' preoccupation with one another as deliverance and safety for themselves, like the ascetic's escape from the thief and the demon when they disagreed over him." The king asked: "How was that?"

The minister said: "They relate that an ascetic received a milk cow from a man and led her home. A thief who wanted to steal her came upon him, and a demon who wanted to carry him off followed him. The demon asked the thief: 'Who are you?' He replied: 'I am a thief. I want to steal the ascetic's cow when he sleeps. Who are you?' He answered: 'I am a demon. I want to seize him when he sleeps and carry him away.' In this way they reached the house. The ascetic went in, and they entered behind him. He brought the cow inside, tied her in a corner, ate supper, and slept.

"The thief and demon began discussing their plans and disagreed about who should act first. The demon said to the thief: 'If you begin by taking the cow, he may wake and cry out. People will gather, and I shall not be able to seize him. Wait until I have taken him, then do as you wish.' The thief feared that if the demon began by carrying off the ascetic, the man might wake and prevent him from taking the cow. He said: 'No, you must wait until I have taken the cow, then do as you wish.' They continued arguing until the thief shouted: 'Ascetic, wake up! This demon wants to carry you off!' The demon shouted: 'Ascetic, wake up! This thief wants to steal your cow!' Their voices woke the ascetic and his neighbors, and the two villains fled."

The first minister, who had advised killing the crow, said: "I think this crow has deceived you, and his words have taken hold in the minds of the foolish among you. Now you wish to apply a policy where it does not belong. Slowly, slowly, O king, before adopting this view!" The king paid no attention and ordered the crow carried to the owls' dwellings, honored, and well cared for.

One day the crow said to the king, in the presence of a company of owls including the minister who had advised killing him: "O king, you know what I suffered at the crows' hands. My heart will find no rest until I take revenge upon them. I have considered the matter and find I cannot accomplish my desire because I am a crow. It is related of the learned that they have said: Whoever willingly burns himself has offered God the greatest sacrifice, and no prayer he makes then goes unanswered. If the king thinks fit, let him command me to burn myself and pray to my Lord to turn me into an owl, so that my hostility toward the crows may be fiercer and my strength against them greater, and perhaps I may avenge myself upon them!"

The minister who had advised killing him said: "In the good you display and the evil you conceal, you resemble nothing so much as wine of pleasant taste and fragrance in which poison has been steeped. Do you imagine that if we burned your body with fire, your essence and nature would change? Would your character not go with you wherever you went, and afterward return to your origin and inward disposition? You are like the mouse who was given a choice of husbands among the sun, wind, cloud, and mountain, but chose none except the rat." He was asked: "How was that?"

He said: "They relate that there was an ascetic whose prayers were answered. One day he was sitting by the seashore when a kite passed carrying a baby mouse in its claw. The mouse fell near the ascetic. Compassion moved him, and he took it, wrapped it in a leaf, and carried it home. Then he feared that raising it would trouble his family, so he prayed to his Lord to turn it into a girl. It became a beautiful girl. He took her to his wife and said: 'This is my daughter. Treat her as you would my child.'

"When she grew up, the ascetic said: 'Daughter, choose whom you like, and I shall marry you to him.' She answered: 'Since you give me the choice, I choose a husband who is the strongest of all things.' The ascetic said: 'Perhaps you mean the sun!' He went to the sun and said: 'Great creature, I have a girl who seeks a husband stronger than all things. Will you marry her?' The sun replied: 'I shall direct you to something stronger than I: the cloud that covers me, repels the heat of my rays, and obscures the beams of my light.'

"The ascetic went to the cloud and said what he had said to the sun. The cloud answered: 'I shall direct you to something stronger than I. Go to the wind, which drives me forward and backward and carries me east and west.' The ascetic went to the wind and spoke as he had to the cloud. The wind said: 'I shall direct you to something stronger than I: the mountain, which I cannot move.' He went to the mountain and repeated his request. The mountain answered: 'I shall direct you to something stronger than I: the rat, against which I cannot defend myself when it tunnels into me and makes me its dwelling.'

"The ascetic went to the rat and asked: 'Will you marry this girl?' The rat replied: 'How can I marry her when my burrow is narrow? A rat marries a mouse.' With the girl's consent, the ascetic prayed to his Lord to turn her into a mouse as she had been. God restored her original nature, and she went away with the rat. Such is your case, deceiver."

The owl king paid no heed to these words. He treated the crow gently and showed him ever greater honor. When the crow's life had become comfortable, his feathers had grown back, and he had discovered all he wished to learn, he slipped away. He brought his companions what he had seen and heard and told the king: "I have completed what I intended. Nothing remains but for you to listen and obey." The king answered: "The troops and I are under your command. Direct us as you wish."

The crow said: "The owls are at such-and-such a place on a mountain with abundant firewood. There is a flock of sheep there with a shepherd, and we shall find fire there. We shall throw it into the owls' openings, cast dry wood upon it, and take turns beating our wings over it until the wood is ablaze. Those who come out will burn, and those who remain inside will die from the smoke where they are." The crows did this, destroyed every one of the owls, and returned to their homes safe and secure.

The crow king said to that crow: "How did you endure the owls' company, when the good cannot bear the company of the wicked?" The crow replied: "What you say is true, O king. But when a dreadful and grave matter confronts the wise, and he fears that failure to endure it will bring destruction upon himself and his people, he does not shrink from the hardship of patience. He hopes that patience will be followed by a good outcome and abundant benefit. Thus he finds no pain in it, nor does his spirit dislike submitting to someone beneath him, until he reaches his goal and rejoices in the conclusion of his affair and the result of his endurance."

The king said: "Tell me about the owls' intelligence." The crow answered: "I found no wise one among them except the minister who urged them to kill me. He pressed them to do so repeatedly, yet his opinion carried the least weight. They did not consider his advice or remember that I had held rank among the crows and was counted among their counselors. They did not fear my cunning and stratagems, accept the counsel of their sincere and concerned adviser, or conceal their secrets from me. The learned have said that a king should safeguard his affairs from informers and reveal none of his secret places to them."

The king said: "To my mind, nothing destroyed the owls but error, their king's weak judgment, and his agreement with bad ministers." The crow replied: "You speak truly, O king. Few gain wealth without becoming overbearing; few eat excessively without falling ill; and few trust bad ministers and escape ruin. It has been said: Let the arrogant not hope for good praise; the deceitful, for many friends; the ill-mannered, for honor; the miserly, for generosity; the greedy, for few sins; or the scheming king, careless of affairs and weak in ministers, for enduring kingship and a prosperous people."

The king said: "You endured severe hardship in accommodating yourself to the owls and humbling yourself before them." The crow answered: "Whoever endures hardship in hope of benefit, sets aside pride and indignation, and disciplines himself to patience will praise the consequence of his judgment, just as the black snake patiently carried the king of the frogs upon his back and thereby found food and survived." The king asked: "How was that?"

The crow said: "They relate that a black snake grew old, his sight weakened, and his strength left him. He could neither hunt nor obtain food. He crawled about seeking something to live on until he reached a spring full of frogs. He had visited it before and obtained his sustenance from its frogs. He threw himself down near them, displaying sorrow and dejection. A frog asked: 'Black snake, why do I see you sad and miserable?' He replied: 'Who has more cause for lasting sorrow than I? Most of my living came from the frogs I caught. But an affliction befell me that has forbidden me frogs, so that even when I encounter one I cannot seize it.'

"The frog went to the frog king and gave him the glad news of what the snake had said. The king asked the snake: 'What happened to you?' He answered: 'Some days ago, toward evening, I was pursuing a frog. I drove it into an ascetic's house and followed it into the darkness. The ascetic's son was in the house. I encountered his finger, mistook it for the frog, and bit him, and he died. I fled, and the ascetic followed my trail, prayed against me, and cursed me. He said: "As you unjustly and aggressively killed my innocent son, I pray that you be humbled and become a mount for the king of the frogs, unable to catch or eat any of them except those their king gives you in charity." So I have come for you to ride me, acknowledging this sentence and accepting it.'

"The frog king desired to ride the black snake, imagining it a source of pride, honor, and exaltation. He mounted, and found it pleasant. The snake said: 'O king, you know I am deprived of food. Assign me sustenance on which to live.' The frog king replied: 'By my life, you must have food to support you if you are my mount.' He ordered two frogs to be taken daily and given to the snake. The snake lived on this. Submission to a lowly enemy did not harm him; rather, he profited from it and gained food and a livelihood.

"Such was my patience in what I endured, seeking this great benefit in which we have gained security, victory, the destruction of the enemy, and relief from him. I have found that the overthrow achieved by gentleness and tact is quicker and more destructive to an enemy than an overthrow by open force. Fire, with all its fierceness and heat, when it strikes a tree burns only what is above the ground; water, cold and gentle, uproots what is beneath the ground. It is said that four things must never be dismissed because they are small: fire, illness, an enemy, and debt."

The crow continued: "All this is due to the king's judgment, instruction, and happy fortune. It has been said: When two people seek a thing, the more honorable obtains it. If they are equal in honor, the more determined obtains it; if equal in determination, the more fortunate. It has also been said: Whoever makes war upon a prudent, intelligent, humble king, whom prosperity does not intoxicate and adversity does not bewilder, invites death upon himself. This is especially true when the king is like you, O king: one who knows the duties of action and the proper places for severity and gentleness, anger and satisfaction, haste and patience, and who considers today's and tomorrow's affairs and the consequences of his deeds."

The king said to the crow: "Rather, this came about through your judgment, intelligence, loyal counsel, and auspicious fortune. The opinion of one intelligent, resolute man is more effective in destroying an enemy than great armies of courageous, valiant men with numbers and equipment. What astonishes me about you is that you stayed so long among the owls, hearing harsh words, yet never betrayed yourself to them by a word!"

The crow answered: "I always held fast to your instruction, O king, treating those near and far with gentleness, tact, the utmost effort, and accommodation." The king said: "Today I have found you to be a man of action, while other ministers are men of words whose consequences are not praiseworthy. God has bestowed upon us through you a great favor. Before it, we found no pleasure in food or drink, sleep or rest. It has been said: The sick person finds no pleasure in food or sleep until he recovers; nor the greedy man whose ruler has aroused his hopes for wealth and an office in his gift, until the ruler fulfills the promise; nor the man relentlessly pursued by an enemy whom he fears morning and evening, until his heart is relieved of him. Whoever lays down a heavy burden eases himself, and whoever is secure from his enemy has a heart refreshed."

The crow said: "I ask God, who destroyed your enemy, to let you enjoy your rule, to make it a source of welfare for your subjects, and to let them share in the joy of your kingship. If a king's rule brings no delight to his subjects' eyes, he is like the wattle of a goat that someone sucks, thinking it a teat of the udder, only to find no nourishment there."

The king said: "Good minister, what was the conduct of the owls and their king in war and in their other affairs?" The crow answered: "His conduct was one of insolence, wantonness, conceit, incapacity, and boasting, along with other blameworthy qualities. All his companions and ministers resembled him except the minister who advised killing me. He was wise, intelligent, philosophical, resolute, and learned, rarely equaled in loftiness of purpose, completeness of understanding, and excellence of judgment."

The king asked: "What quality did you see in him that most clearly showed his intelligence?" The crow said: "Two qualities. One was his opinion that I should be killed. The other was that he did not withhold his counsel from his master even when it was undervalued. His speech was not violent or harsh but gentle and mild. Sometimes he informed the king of a fault without explicitly stating the true situation. Instead, he offered examples and described another person's defect, so that the king recognized his own fault yet found no grounds for anger against him.

"Among the things I heard him say to his king was this: A king must not neglect his office, for it is a great matter attained by few and secured only through resolve. Kingship is precious. Whoever gains it should guard and fortify it well. It has been said that in its brief endurance it resembles the fleeting shade of a water-lily leaf; in the ease of its disappearance and the speed of its coming and going, the wind; in its lack of stability, an intelligent person among the base; and in the swiftness of its vanishing, bubbles formed on water by falling rain."

This is the example of enemies whom one must not trust, even when they display affection and humility.

blocks.text: قال دبشليم الملك لبيدبا الفيلسوف: قد سمعت هذا المثل فاضرب لي مثل الرجل الذي يطلب الحاجة فإذا ظفر بها أضاعها.
قال الفيلسوف: إن طلب الحاجة أهون من الاحتفاظ بها، ومَنْ ظفر بالحاجة ثم لم يحسن القيام بها أصابه ما أصاب الغيلم: قال الملك: وكيف كان ذلك؟

قال بيدبا: زعموا أن قردًا كان ملك القردة يقال له ماهر، وكان قد كبر وهرم، فوثب عليه قرد شاب من بيت المملكة فتغلَّب عليه وأخذ مكانه؛ فخرج هاربًا على وجهه حتى انتهى إلى الساحل، فوجد شجرة من شجرة التين، فارتقى إليها وجعلها مقامه، فبينما هو ذات يوم يأكل من ذلك التين إذا سقطت من يده تينة في الماء فسمع لها صوتًا وإيقاعًا؛ فجعل يأكل ويرمي في الماء، فأطربه ذلك، فأكثر من تطريح التين في الماء وثمَّ غيلم كلَّما وقعت تينة أكلها، فلمَّا كثر ذلك ظنَّ أن القرد إنما يفعل ذلك لأجله؛ فرغب في مصادقته وأنس إليه وكلَّمه، وألف كل واحد منهما صاحبه.

وطالت غيبة الغيلم عن زوجته؛ فجزعت عليه وشكت ذلك إلى جارة لها وقالت: قد خفت أن يكون قد عرض له عارض سوء فاغتاله، فقالت لها: إن زوجك في الساحل قد ألف قردًا وألفه القرد فهو مؤاكله ومشاربه، وهو الذي قطعه عنك، ولا يقدر أن يقيم عندك حتى تحتالي لهلاك القرد. قالت: وكيف أصنع؟ قالت جارتها: إذا وصل إليك فتمارضي فإذا سألك عن حالك فقولي إن الأطباء وصفوا لي قلب قردٍ.

ثم إن الغيلم انطلق بعد مدَّة إلى منزله فوجد زوجته سيئة الحال مهمومة. فقال لها: ما لي أراك هكذا؟ فأجابته جارتها وقالت: إن زوجتك مريضة مسكينة، وقد وصف لها الأطباء قلب قرد، وليس لها دواء سواه. قال الغيلم: هذا أمر عسير، من أين لنا قلب قرد، ونحن في الماء؟ وبقي متحيرًا. ثم قال في نفسه: ما لي قدرة على ذلك إلاَّ أن أغدر بخليلي وصاحبي. وإثمه عندي شديد، وأشدُّ من ذلك هلاك زوجتي؛ لأن الزوجة الصالحة لا يعدلها شيء لأنها عون على أمر الدُّنيا والآخرة.

ثم عاد إلى الساحل حزينًا كئيبًا مفكرًا في نفسه كيف يصنع. فقال له القرد: يا أخي ما حبسك عني؟ قال له الغيلم: ما حبسني عنك إلاَّ حيائي فلم أعرف كيف أكافئك على إحسانك إليَّ، وأريد أن تتم إحسانك إليَّ بزيارتك لي في منزلي، فإني ساكن في جزيرة طيبة الفاكهة، فاركب ظهري لأسبح بك، فإن أفضل ما يلتمسه المرء من أخلائه أن يغشوا منزله وينالوا من طعامه وشرابه ويعرفهم أهله وولده وجيرانه، وأنت لم تطأ منزلي ولم تذق لي طعامًا ولا شرابًا؛ وذلك منقصة وعار عليَّ. قال له القرد: وما يريد المرء من خليله إلاَّ أن يبذل له ودَّه ويُصفِي له قلبه وما سوى ذلك ففضول.

قال الغيلم: نعم. غير أن الاجتماع على الطعام والشراب آكد للمودة والأنس؛ لأنا نرى الدواب إذا اعتلفت معًا ألف بعضها بعضًا، وكان يقال: لا ينبغي للعاقل أن يلحَّ على إخوانه في المسألة، فإن العجل إذا أكثر مصَّ ضرع أمه نطحته.

فرغب القرد في الذهاب معه فقال: حبًا وكرامة، ونزل فركب ظهر الغيلم فسبح به، حتى إذا تجاوز قليلاً عرض له قبح ما أضمر في نفسه من الغدر، فنكس رأسه ووقف وقال في نفسه: كيف أغدر بخليلي لكلمة قالتها امرأة من الجاهلات؟ وما أدري لعل جارتي قد خدعتني وكذبت بما روت عن الأطباء. فإن الذَّهب يجرَّب بالنار، والرجال بالأخذ والعطاء، والدواب بالحمل والجري. ولا يقدر أحد أن يجرِّب مكر النساء ولا يقدر على كيدهنَّ وكثرة حيلهنَّ.

فقال له القرد: ما لي أراك مهتمًا؟ قال الغيلم: إنما همي لأني ذكرت أن زوجتي شديدة المرض وذلك يمنعني من كثيرٍ مما أريد أن أبلغه من كرامتك وملاطفتك. قال القرد: إن الذي أعرف من حرصك على كرامتي يكفيك مئونة التكلُّف.

قال الغيلم: أجل. ومضى بالقرد ساعة ثمَّ توقَّف به ثانية؛ فساء ظنُّ القرد وقال في نفسه: ما احتباس الغيلم وإبطاؤه إلاَّ لأمر. ولست آمنًا أن يكون قلبه قد تغيَّر لي وحال عن مودَّتي فأراد بي سوءًا. فإنه لا شيء أخف وأسرع تقلُّبا من القلب. وقد يقال ينبغي للعاقل أن لا يغفل عن التماس ما في نفس أهله وولده وإخوانه وصديقه عند كل أمر، وفي كل لحظة وكلمة، وعند القيام والقعود، وعلى كل حالٍ. فإن ذلك كله يشهد على ما في القلوب، وقد قالت العلماء: إذا دخل قلب الصديق من صديقه ريبة فليأخذ بالحزم في التحفُّظ منه، وليتفقد ذلك في لحظاته وحالاته، فإن كان ما يظنُّ حقًا ظفر بالسلامة، وإن كان باطلاً ظفر بالحزم ولم يَضُرَّه ذلك.

ثم قال للغيلم: ما يحبسك وما لي أراك مهتمًا كأنك تحدِّث نفسك مرة أخرى؟ قال: يهمني أنك تأتي منزلي فلا تجد أمري كما أحبُّ لأن زوجتي مريضة. قال القرد: لا تغتم فإن الغمُّ لا يغني عنك شيئًا، ولكن التمس ما يصلح زوجتك من الأدوية والأغذية، فإنه يقال: ليبذل ذوو المال مالهم في أربعة مواضع: في الصدقة، وفي وقت الحاجة، وعلى البنين، وعلى الأزواج ولا سيما إذا كنَّ صالحات. قال الغيلم: صدقت. وقد قالت الأطباء: إنه لا دواء لها إلاَّ قلب قرد.

فقال القرد في نفسه: واسوءتاه! لقد أدركني الحرص والشَّره على كبر سني حتى وقعت في شرِّ ورطه، ولقد صدق الذي قال يعيش القانع الراضي مستريحًا مطمئنًا، وذو الحرص والشَّره يعيش ما عاش في تعب ونصب. وإني قد احتجت الآن إلى عقلي في التماس المخرج مما وقعت فيه.

ثم قال للغيلم: وما منعك، أصلحك الله، أن تعلمني عند منزلي حتى كنت أحمل قلبي معي؟ فإن هذه سُنَّة فينا معاشر القردة إذا خرج أحدنا لزيارة صديق له خلَّف قلبه عند أهله أو في موضعه لننظر إذا نظرنا إلى حرم المزور وليس قلوبنا معنا. قال الغيلم: وأين قلبك الآن؟ قال: خلَّفته في الشجرة، فإن شئت فارجع بي إلى الشجرة حتى آتيك به.

ففرح الغيلم بذلك وقال: لقد وافقني صاحبي بدون أن أغدر به، ثم رجع بالقرد إلى مكانه، فلمَّا قارب الساحل وثب عن ظهره فارتقى الشجرة، فلمَّا أبطأ على الغيلم ناداه: يا خليلي احمل قلبك وانزل فقد حبستني. فقال القرد: هيهات! أتظن أني كالحمار الذي زعم ابن آوى أنه لم يكن له قلب ولا أذنان؟ قال الغيلم: وكيف كان ذلك؟

قال القرد: زعموا أنه كان أسد في أجمة، وكان معه ابن آوى يأكل من فضلات طعامه. فأصاب الأسد جرب وضعف شديدً وجهد فلم يستطع الصيد.. فقال له ابن آوى: ما بالك يا سيد السباع قد تغيَّرت أحوالك؟ قال: هذا الجرب الذي قد جهدني وليس له دواء إلاَّ قلب حمار وأذناه.

قال ابن آوى: ما أيسر هذا! وقد عرفت بمكان كذا حمارًا مع قصَّار يحمل عليه ثيابه وأنا آتيك به. ثم دلف إلى الحمار فأتاه وسلَّم عليه وقال له: ما لي أراك مهزولاً؟ قال: لسوء تدبير صاحبي، فإنه لا يزال يجيع بطني ويثقل ظهري، وما تجتمع هاتان الحالتان على جسم إلاَّ أنحلتاه وأسقمتاه. فقال له: كيف ترضى المقام معه على هذا؟ قال: ما لي حيلة للهرب منه فلست أتوجَّه إلى جهة إلاَّ أضرَّ بي إنسان فكدني وأجاعني.
قال ابن آوى: فأنا أدلك على مكان معزول عن الناس لا يمرُّ به إنسان، خصيب المرعى فيه عانة من الحمر ترعى آمنة مطمئنة. قال الحمار: وما يحبسنا عنها؟ فانطلق بنا إليها.
فانطلق به نحو الأسد، وتقدَّم ابن آوى ودخل الغابة على الأسد فأخبره بمكان الحمار.

فخرج إليه وأراد أن يثب عليه فلم يستطع لضعفه وتخلَّص الحمار منه فأفلت هلعًا على وجهه. فلمَّا رأى ابن آوى أن الأسد لم يقدر على الحمار قال له: يا سيد السباع أعجزت إلى هذه الغاية؟ فقال له: إن جئتني به مرَّة أخرى فلن ينجو مني أبدًا.
فمضى ابن آوى إلى الحمار فقال له: ما الذي جرى عليك؟ إن أحد الحمر رآك غريبًا فخرج يتلقاك مرحبًا بك، ولو ثبت لآنسك ومضى بك إلى أصحابه.

فلمَّا سمع الحمار ذلك ولم يكن رأى أسدًا قط صدَّق ما قاله ابن آوى وأخذ طريقه إلى الأسد. فسبقه ابن آوى إلى الأسد وأعلمه بمكانه وقال له: استعد له فقد خدعته لك لا يدركنَّك الضعف في هذه النوبة. فإنه إن أفلت لن يعود معي أبدًا والفرص لا تصاب في كل وقت.

فجاش جأش الأسد لتحريض ابن آوى له وخرج إلى موضع الحمار، فلمَّا بصر به عاجله بوثبة افترسه بها. ثم قال: قد ذكرت الأطباء أنه لا يؤكل إلاَّ بعد الاغتسال والطهور. فاحتفظ به حتى أعود فآكل قلبه وأذنيه وأترك ما سوى ذلك قوتًا لك.
فلمَّا ذهب الأسد ليغتسل عمد ابن آوى إلى الحمار فأكل قلبه وأذنيه رجاء أن يتطير الأسد منه فلا يأكل منه شيئًا.
ثم إن الأسد رجع إلى مكانه فقال لابن آوى: أين قلب الحمار وأذناه؟ قال ابن آوى: ألم تعلم أنه لو كان له قلب يعقل به وأذنان يسمع بهما لم يرجع إليك بعدما أفلت ونجا من الهلكة!

وإنما ضربت لك هذا المثل لتعلم أني لست كذلك الحمار الذي زعم ابن آوى أنه لم يكن له قلب ولا أذنان. ولكنك احتلت عليَّ وخدعتني فخدعتك بمثل خديعتك واستدركت فرط أمري. وقد قيل: إن الذي يفسده الحلم لا يصلحه إلاَّ العلم.

قال الغيلم: صدقت! إلاَّ أن الرجل الصالح يعترف بزلته، وإذا أذنب ذنبًا لم يستحي أن يؤدَّب لصدقه في قوله وفعله، وإن وقع في ورطة أمكنه التخلُّص منها بحيلته وعقله، كالرجل الذي يعثر على الأرض وعليها يعتمد في نهوضه.
فهذا مثل الرجل الذي يطلب الحاجة فإذا ظفر بها أضاعها.

english.text: The Monkey and the Tortoise

King Dabshalim said to Bidpai the philosopher, “I have heard this example. Give me an example of a man who seeks something he needs, obtains it, and then loses it.”

The philosopher said, “Seeking something is easier than preserving it. Whoever obtains what he needs but does not manage it properly meets the fate of the tortoise.”

“How was that?” asked the king.

Bidpai said, “They say that a monkey named Mahir was king of the monkeys. He had grown old and infirm when another monkey of the royal family rose against him, defeated him, and took his place. He fled aimlessly until he reached the seashore. There he found a fig tree, climbed into it, and made it his home.

“One day, as he was eating its figs, a fig fell from his hand into the water. He heard its sound and rhythm, and began eating and throwing figs into the water. The sound delighted him, so he threw in many figs. A tortoise was there and ate each fig that fell. When this continued, he thought the monkey was doing it for his sake. He wished to befriend him, became familiar with him, and spoke to him. Each grew fond of the other.

“The tortoise stayed away from his wife a long time. She became anxious and complained to a neighbor, saying, ‘I fear some evil has overtaken him and carried him off.’

“The neighbor said, ‘Your husband is at the shore. He has become fond of a monkey, and the monkey of him. They eat and drink together. That is what has kept him away from you. He will not remain with you until you devise a way to destroy the monkey.’

“‘What should I do?’ she asked.

“Her neighbor said, ‘When he comes to you, pretend to be ill. When he asks how you are, say that the physicians have prescribed a monkey’s heart.’

“After some time the tortoise went home and found his wife in a wretched, troubled state. He asked, ‘Why do I see you like this?’ Her neighbor answered, ‘Your wife is ill and helpless. The physicians have prescribed a monkey’s heart, and there is no other cure.’

“The tortoise said, ‘That is difficult. Where can we find a monkey’s heart when we live in the water? But I shall devise a plan against my friend.’

“He went to the shore. The monkey said, ‘Brother, what has kept you from me?’

“The tortoise said, ‘Only my embarrassment. I did not know how to repay your kindness. I want you to complete it by visiting me at home. I live on an island with delicious fruit.’

“The monkey climbed onto the tortoise’s back, and he swam away with him. As he swam, the ugliness of the treachery he had concealed within himself came before his mind, and he lowered his head.

“The monkey asked, ‘Why do you look troubled?’

“The tortoise said, ‘I am troubled because I remembered that my wife is very ill. That will prevent me from doing much of what I desire in my eagerness to honor and entertain you.’

“The monkey said, ‘What I already know of your desire to honor me spares you the trouble of elaborate preparations.’

“‘Yes,’ said the tortoise. He carried the monkey onward a while, then stopped again. The monkey grew suspicious and thought, ‘There must be a reason for the tortoise’s hesitation and delay. I cannot be sure that his heart has not changed toward me, that his affection has not altered, and that he does not intend me harm. Nothing is lighter or quicker to change than the heart. It has been said that a sensible person should never neglect to discover what lies in the minds of his family, children, brothers, and friends, in every affair, glance, and word, when they rise or sit, and in every condition. All these reveal what is in the heart. The learned have said: when suspicion of a friend enters a friend’s heart, he should take prudent precautions and examine his glances and behavior. If his suspicion is true, he gains safety; if false, he has acted cautiously and suffered no harm.’

“He said to the tortoise, ‘What is delaying you? Why do you look troubled, as though talking to yourself again?’

“‘It troubles me that you will come to my home and not find my affairs as I would wish, because my wife is ill.’

“The monkey said, ‘Do not worry. Worry does you no good. Seek the medicines and foods that will restore your wife. It is said that a wealthy person should spend his wealth in four places: charity, necessity, children, and wives.’

“The tortoise said, ‘You are right. The physicians have said that her only remedy is a monkey’s heart.’

“The monkey thought, ‘Alas! Greed and appetite have overtaken me in my old age and brought me into a terrible predicament. True was the saying: the contented, satisfied person lives peacefully and securely, while the greedy and ravenous person spends his life in toil and weariness. Now I need my intelligence to find a way out of what has happened.’

“He said to the tortoise, ‘Why did you not tell me while I was at home? I could have brought my heart with me. It is our custom, among monkeys, to leave our hearts with our families or in our dwelling when we go to visit a friend, so that, if we look upon the women of our host’s household, our hearts are not with us.’

“The tortoise asked, ‘Where is your heart now?’

“‘I left it in the tree. If you wish, take me back to the tree and I will bring it to you.’

“The tortoise rejoiced and thought, ‘My friend has agreed to my wish without my betraying him.’ He took the monkey back to his place. When the monkey delayed returning, he called, ‘My dear friend, bring your heart and come down. You have kept me waiting.’

“The monkey said, ‘Far from it! Do you think I am like the donkey of whom the jackal claimed that he had neither heart nor ears?’

“‘How was that?’ asked the tortoise.

“The monkey said, ‘They say that a lion lived in a thicket, accompanied by a jackal who ate the leftovers of his meals. The lion developed mange and became so weak that he could not hunt.

“‘The jackal asked, “What is wrong, lord of beasts? Your condition has changed.”

“‘The lion said, “This mange has exhausted me. There is no remedy except a donkey’s heart and ears.”

“‘The jackal said, “How easy that is! I know a donkey in a certain place belonging to a fuller who loads his clothes upon it. I will bring it to you.”

“‘He went stealthily to the donkey, greeted him, and asked, “Why do you look so thin?”

“‘“My master feeds me nothing.”

“‘“How can you be content to remain with him in such a state?”

“‘“I have no way to escape. Wherever I turn, some person beats me, works me hard, and starves me.”

“‘The jackal said, “I will show you a place apart from people, where no human passes. Its pasture is rich, and a herd of donkeys lives there, more beautiful and fat than any eye has seen.”

“‘The donkey said, “What is keeping us from them? Let us go.”

“‘The jackal led him toward the lion, went ahead into the wood, and told the lion where the donkey was. The lion came out and tried to spring upon him, but his weakness prevented him. The donkey broke away and fled in terror.

“‘Seeing that the lion had failed, the jackal said, “Lord of beasts, have you become as helpless as this?”

“‘The lion answered, “Bring him once more, and he will never escape me.”

“‘The jackal went to the donkey and said, “What happened to you? One of the donkeys saw that you were a stranger and came out to welcome you. If you had stood still, he would have made you feel at home and taken you to his companions.”

“‘The donkey had never seen a lion. He believed the jackal and set off toward him. The jackal told the lion where he was and said, “Prepare yourself. I have deceived him for you. Do not let weakness overcome you this time. If he escapes, he will never return with me.”

“‘The jackal’s urging stirred the lion’s courage. He went to where the donkey was, and, the moment he saw him, sprang upon him and killed him. Then he said, “The physicians said it must not be eaten until after washing and purification. Guard him until I return to eat his heart and ears. I will leave the rest for your food.”

“‘When the lion went to wash, the jackal ate the donkey’s heart and ears, hoping that the lion would regard their absence as an evil omen and eat none of the carcass. The lion asked, “Where are the donkey’s heart and ears?”

“‘The jackal said, “Do you not know that if he had possessed a heart to understand with, and ears to hear with, he would not have returned after escaping you and saving himself from destruction?”

“‘I have told you this example so that you know I am not that donkey, whom the jackal said had no heart or ears. You plotted against me and deceived me, so I answered your deception with its like and recovered what I had nearly lost. It has been said: what forbearance spoils, knowledge alone can set right.’

“The tortoise said, ‘You speak truly. Yet a good man acknowledges his mistake. When he sins, he is not ashamed to be corrected, because he is truthful in word and deed. If he falls into a predicament, he can escape it through ingenuity and intelligence, like a man who stumbles upon the ground and then rises by leaning upon that same ground.’

“This is the example of a man who seeks something, obtains it, and then loses it.”

blocks.text: قال دبشليم الملك لبيدبا الفيلسوف: قد سمعت هذا المثل، فاضرب لي مثل الرجل العجلان في أمره من غير روية ولا نظر في العواقب.
قال الفيلسوف: إنه مَنْ لم يكن في أمره متثبتًا لم يزل نادمًا ويصير أمره إلى ما صار إليه النَّاسك من قتل ابن عرس وقد كان له ودودًا. قال الملك وكيف كان ذلك؟

قال الفيلسوف: زعموا أن ناسكًا من النُسَّاك كان بأرض جرجان، وكانت له امرأة صالحة لها معه صحبة، فمكثا زمانًا لم يرزقا ولدًا، ثم حملت بعد الإياس، فسُرَّت المرأة وسُرَّ النَّاسك بذلك وحمد الله تعالى وسأله أن يكون الحمل ذكرًا، وقال لزوجته: أبشري فإني أرجو أن يكون غلامًا فيه لنا منافع وقرَّة عينٍ، أختار له أحسن الأسماء، وأحضر له جميع المؤدِّبين.
فقالت المرأة: ما يحملك أيها الرجل على أن تتكلم بما لا تدري أيكون أم لا؟
ومَنْ فعل ذلك أصابه ما أصاب النَّاسك الذي أهرق على رأسه السمن والعسل. قال لها وكيف كان ذلك؟
قالت: زعموا أن ناسكًا كان يجري عليه من بيت رجل تاجر في كل يوم رزق من السمن والعسل، وكان يأكل منه قوته وحاجته ويرفع الباقي ويجعله في جرَّة فيعلِّقها في وتد في ناحية البيت حتى امتلأت.

فبينما النَّاسك ذات يوم مستلقٍ على ظهره والعكَّازة في يده والجرَّة معلَّقة فوق رأسه تفكَّر في غلاء السمن والعسل فقال: سأبيع ما في هذه الجرَّة بدينار وأشتري به عشر أعنز فيحبلن ويلدن في كل خمسة أشهر مرَّة. ولا تلبث إلاَّ قليلاً حتى تصير معزًا كثيرًا إذا ولدت أولادها.

ثم حرَّر على هذا النحو بسنين فوجد ذلك أكثر من أربعمئة عنز. فقال: أنا أشتري بها مئة من البقر بكل أربع أعنز ثورًا أو بقرة، وأشتري أرضًا وبذرًا، وأستأجر أكرة وأزرع على الثيران وأنتفع بألبان الإناث ونتائجها. فلا تأتي عليَّ خمس سنين إلاَّ وقد أصبت من الزرع مالاً كثيرًا؛ فأبني بيتًا فاخرًا وأشتري إماءً وعبيدًا وأتزوَّج امرأة صالحة جميلة فتحمل ثم تأتي بغلام سري نجيب فاختار له أحسن الأسماء، فإذا ترعرع أدَّبته وأحسنت تأديبه، وأشدد عليه في ذلك، فإن قبل مني وإلاَّ ضربته بهذه العكَّازة. وأشار بيده إلى الجرَّة فكسرها فسال ما فيها على وجهه.

وإنما ضربت لك هذا المثل؛ لكي لا تعجل بذكر ما لا ينبغي ذكره وما لا تدري أيصحُّ أم لا يصحُّ. ولكن ادعُ ربَّك وتوسَّل إليه وتوكَّل عليه. فإن التصاوير في الحائط إنما هي ما دام بناؤه قائمًا فإذا وقع وتهدَّم لم يُقدَر عليها، فاتَّعظ النَّاسك بما حكت زوجته.
ثم إن المرأة ولدت غلامًا جميلاً؛ ففرح به أبوه، وبعد أيام حان لها أن تغتسل، فقالت المرأة للنَّاسك: اقعد عند ابنك حتى أذهب إلى الحمام فأغتسل وأعود.

ثم إنها انطلقت إلى الحمام وخلَّفت زوجها والغلام. فلم يلبث أن جاء رسول الملك يستدعيه ولم يجد مَنْ يخلفه عند ابنه غير ابن عرس داجن عنده كان قد ربَّاه صغيرًا فهو عنده عديل ولده، فتركه النَّاسك عند الصبي وأغلق عليهما البيت وذهب مع الرسول؛ فخرج من بعض أحجار البيت حيَّة سوداء فدنت من الغلام؛ فضربها ابن عرس فوثب عليها فقتلها ثم قطعها وامتلأ فمه من دمها.

ثم جاء النَّاسك وفتح الباب فالتقاه ابن عرس كالمشير له بما صنع من قتل الحيَّة، فلمَّا رآه ملوثًا بالدم وهو مذعور طار عقله وظنَّ أنه قد خنق ولده، ولم يتثبَّت في أمره ولم يتروَ فيه حتى يعلم حقيقة الحال ويعمل بغير ما ظنَّ من ذلك ولكن عجَّل على ابن عرس وضربه بعكَّازة كانت في يده على أمِّ رأسه فمات، ودخل النَّاسك فرأى الغلام سليمًا حيًا وعنده أسود مقطع. فلما عرف القصة وتبيَّن له سوء فعله في العجلة لطم على رأسه وقال: ليتني لم أرزق هذا الولد ولم أغدر هذا الغدر!.

ودخلت امرأته فوجدته على تلك الحال فقالت له: ما شأنك؟ فأخبرها بالخبر من حسن فعل ابن عرس وسوء مكافأته له. فقالت: هذه ثمرة العجلة؛ لأن الأمر إذا فرط مثل الكلام إذا خرج، والسهم إذا مرق لا مردَّ له. فهذا مثل مَنْ لا يتثبَّت في أمره بل يفعل أغراضه بالسرعة.

english.text: The Ascetic and the Weasel

King Dabshalim said to Bidpai the philosopher, “I have heard this example. Give me an example of a man who acts hastily, without reflection or consideration of consequences.”

The philosopher said, “Whoever does not proceed carefully is always regretting his actions. His affairs end like those of the ascetic who killed the weasel that had been his affectionate friend.”

“How was that?” asked the king.

The philosopher said, “They say that an ascetic in the land of Jurjan had a beautiful wife. They lived for a long time without being granted a child. After they had despaired, she conceived. Both she and the ascetic rejoiced. He praised God Most High and prayed that the child would be male. He told his wife, ‘Be glad! I hope it will be a boy who brings us benefit and delight. I shall choose the finest name for him and assemble all the teachers to instruct him.’

“His wife said, ‘What makes you speak of something when you do not know whether it will happen? Whoever does that meets the fate of the ascetic who spilled butter and honey over his own head.’

“‘How was that?’ he asked.

“She said, ‘They say that an ascetic received a daily allowance of clarified butter and honey from a merchant’s household. He ate what he needed and saved the remainder in a jar, which he hung on a peg in a corner of the house until it was full. One day he lay upon his back, a staff in his hand and the jar hanging above his head. Thinking of the high price of butter and honey, he said:

“‘“I will sell what is in this jar for a dinar and buy ten she-goats. They will conceive and bear young every five months. Before long, when their offspring reproduce, they will become a great flock.”

“‘He calculated in this manner over several years and arrived at more than four hundred goats. He said, “With them I will buy a hundred cattle. I will buy land and seed, hire farm workers, and plow with the oxen. I will benefit from the cows’ milk and offspring. Before five years have passed, I will have gained great wealth from farming. I will build a splendid house, buy female and male servants, and marry a lovely, beautiful woman. Then she will bear a noble, intelligent boy. I will choose the finest name for him. When he grows, I will educate him well and be strict with him. If he obeys me, well and good; otherwise I will strike him with this staff.”

“‘He gestured toward the jar and broke it. Everything in it poured over his face. I tell you this example so that you will not rush to speak of what should not yet be spoken of, when you do not know whether it will happen.’

“The ascetic took warning from his wife’s story. In time she gave birth to a beautiful boy, and his father rejoiced. Some days later, the time came for her purification. She told the ascetic, ‘Stay with your son while I go to the bathhouse, wash, and return.’ She went, leaving her husband and the boy.

“Before long a messenger from the king arrived to summon him. He could find no one to leave with his son except a tame weasel he had raised from infancy and regarded almost as another child. He left the weasel with the baby, shut them in the house, and went with the messenger.

“A black snake came out from a crevice in the house and approached the boy. The weasel struck it, sprang upon it, killed it, and tore it apart, filling his mouth with its blood.

“The ascetic returned and opened the door. The weasel met him as though bringing the good news that he had killed the snake. Seeing him stained with blood, the ascetic became terrified and lost his reason. He imagined that the weasel had strangled his child. He did not pause or reflect until he knew the truth and could act on something other than supposition. Instead he hastily struck the weasel on the crown of the head with the staff in his hand, and killed him.

“Then he entered and saw the boy alive and unharmed, with a black snake cut to pieces beside him. When he understood what had happened and recognized the evil he had done through haste, he struck his own head and said, ‘Would that I had never been given this child and had not committed this treachery!’

“His wife came in and found him in that state. ‘What is wrong?’ she asked. He told her of the weasel’s good deed and his own evil repayment. She said, ‘This is the fruit of haste.’

“This is the example of one who does not deliberate in his affairs, but carries out his purposes with speed and haste.”

blocks.text: قال دبشليم الملك لبيدبا الفيلسوف: قد سمعت هذا المثل، فاضرب لي مثل رجلٍ كثر أعداؤه وأحدقوا به من كل جانب، فأشرف معهم على الهلاك، فالتمس النجاة والمخرج بموالاة بعض أعدائه ومصالحته؛ فسلم من الخوف وأمن. ثم وفى لمَنْ صالحه منهم، وأخبرني عن موضع الصلح وكيف ينبغي أن يكون.

قال الفيلسوف: إن المودَّة والعداوة لا تثبتان على حالة أبدًا، وربما حالت المودَّة إلى العداوة وصارت العداوة ولاية وصداقة؛ ولهذا حوادث وعلل وتجارب، وذو الرأي يحدث لكل ما يحدث من ذلك رأيًا جديدًا. أمَّا من قبل العدوِّ فبالبأس وأمَّا من قبل الصديق فبالاستئناس، ولا تمنع ذا العقل عداوة كانت في نفسه لعدوِّه من مقاربته والاستنجاد به على دفع مرهوب أو جرِّ مرغوب، ومَنْ عمل في ذلك بالحزم ظفر بحاجته، ومثل ذلك مثل الجرذ والسنور حين وقعا في الورطة فنجوا باصطلاحها جميعًا من الورطة والشدَّة. قال الملك: وكيف كان ذلك؟

قال بيدبا: زعموا أن شجرة عظيمة كان في أصلها جحر سنور يقال له رومي، وكان قريبًا منه جحر جرذ يقال له فريدون، وكان الصيادون كثيرًا ما يتداولون ذلك المكان يصيدون فيه الوحش والطير، فأتى ذات يوم صياد فنصب حبالته قريبًا من موضع رومي فلم يلبث أن وقع فيها؛ فخرج الجرذ يدبُّ ويطلب ما يأكل وهو حذر من رومي فبينما هو يسعى إذ بصر به في الشَّرك فسُرَّ واستبشر، ثم التفت فرأى خلفه ابن عرس يريد أخذه، وفي الشجرة بومًا يريد اختطافه؛ فتحيَّر في أمره وخاف، إن رجع وراءه أخذه ابن عرس، وإن ذهب يمينًا أو شمالاً اختطفه البوم، وإن تقدَّم أمامه افترسه السنُّور.

فقال في نفسه: هذا بلاء قد اكتنفني وشرور تظاهرت عليَّ، ومحن قد أحاطت بي، وبعد ذلك فمعي عقلي فلا يفزعني أمري ولا يهولني شأني ولا يلحقني الدَّهش ولا يذهب قلبي شعاعًا؛ فالعاقل لا يفرق عند سداد رأيه ولا يعزب عنه ذهنه على حال، وإنما العقل شبيه بالبحر الذي لا يدرك غوره، ولا يبلغ البلاء من ذي الرأي مجهوده فيهلكه، وتحقُّق الرجاء لا ينبغي أن يبلغ منه مبلغًا يبطره ويسكره فيُعمِي عليه أمره، ولست أرى لي من هذا البلاء مخلِّصًا إلاَّ مصالحة السنور، فإنه قد نزل به من البلاء مثل ما قد نزل بي أو بعضه، ولعلنا إن سمع كلامي الذي أكلمه به ووعى عني صحيح خطابي ومحض صدقي الذي لا خلاف فيه ولا خداع معه ففهمه وطمع في معونتي إياه نخلص جميعًا.

ثمَّ إنَّ الجرذ دنا من السنور فقال له: كيف حالك؟ قال له السنور: كما تحبُّ في ضنك وضيق، قال: وأنا اليوم شريكك في البلاء، ولست أرجو لنفسي خلاصًا إلاَّ بالذي أرجو لك فيه الخلاص، وكلامي هذا ليس فيه كذب ولا خديعة، وابن عرس ها هو كامن لي، واليوم يرصدني، وكلاهما لي ولك عدوُّ، وإني وإياك وإن كنا مختلفي الطباع لكننا متفقا الحالة.

والذين حالتهم واحدة وطباعهم مختلفة تجمعهم الحالة وإن فرَّقتهم الطباع، فإن أنت جعلت لي الأمان قطعت حبائلك وخلَّصتك من هذه الورطة، فإن كان ذلك تخلَّص كل واحد منا بسبب صاحبه، كالسفينة والرُّكاب في البحر فبالسفينة ينجون وبهم تنجو السفينة.
فلمَّا سمع السنور كلام الجرذ وعرف أنه صادق قال له: إن قولك هذا لشبيه بالحق، وأنا أيضًا راغب فيما أرجو لك ولنفسي به الخلاص، ثم إني إن فعلت ذلك سأشكرك ما بقيت.
قال الجرذ: فإني سأدنو منك فأقطع الحبائل كلها إلاَّ حبلاً واحدًا أبقيه لأستوثق لنفسي منك، وأخذ في تقريض حبائله، ثم إن البوم وابن عرس لمَّا رأيا دنوَّ الجرذ من السنور أيسا منه وانصرفا.

ثم إن الجرذ أبطأ على رومي في قطع الحبائل فقال له: ما لي لا أراك جادًا في قطع حبائلي؟ فإن كنت قد ظفرت بحاجتك فتغيَّرت عما كنت عليه وتوانيت في حاجتي فما ذلك من فعل الصالحين؛ فإن الكريم لا يتوانى في حق صاحبه، وقد كان لك في سابق مودَّتي من الفائدة والنفع ما قد رأيت، وأنت حقيق أن تكافئني بذلك ولا تذكر العداوة التي بيني وبينك، فالذي بيني وبينك من الصلح حقيق أن ينسيك ذلك مع ما في الوفاء من الفضل والأجر وما في الغدر من سوء العاقبة، فإن الكريم لا يكون إلاَّ شكورًا غير حقود تنسيه الخلَّة الواحدة من الإحسان الخلال الكثيرة من الإساءة، وقد يقال: إن أعجل العقوبة عقوبة الغدر، ومَنْ إذا تُضُرِّع إليه وسُئِلَ العفو فلم يرحم ولم يعف فقد غدر.

قال الجرذ: إن الصديق صديقان، طائع ومضطر، وكلاهما يلتمسان المنفعة ويحترسان من المضرَّة، فأمَّا الطائع فيسترسل إليه ويؤمن في جميع الأحوال، وأمَّا المضطر ففي بعض الأحوال يسترسل إليه وفي بعضها يُتحذَّر منه. ولا يزال العاقل يرتهن منه بعض حاجاته لبعض ما يتقي ويخاف، وليس غاية التواصل من كل من المتواصلين إلاَّ طلب عاجل النفع وبلوغ مأموله، وأنا وافٍ لك بما وعدتك ومحترس منك مع ذلك من حيث أخافك تخوُّف أن يصيبني منك ما ألجأني خوفه إلى مصالحتك وألجأك إلى قبول ذلك مني؛ فإن لكل عمل حينًا، فما لم يكن منه في حينه فلا حسن لعاقبته، وأنا قاطع حبائلك كلها، غير أني تارك عقدة أرتهنك بها ولا أقطعها إلاَّ في الساعة التي أعلم أنك فيها عني مشغول وذلك عند معاينتي الصياد.

ثم إن الجرذ أخذ في قطع حبائل السنور، فبينما هو كذلك إذ وافى الصياد. فقال السنور: الآن جاء وقت الجدِّ في قطع حبائلي؛ فجهد الجرذ نفسه في القرض، حتى إذا فرغ وثب السنور إلى الشجرة على دهش من الصياد، ودخل الجرذ بعض الأجحار، وجاء الصياد فأخذ حبائله مقطَّعة ثمَّ انصرف خائبًا.

ثمَّ إنَّ الجرذ خرج بعد ذلك وكره أن يدنو من السنور، فناداه السنور: أيها الصديق الناصح ذو البلاء الحسن عندي، ما منعك من الدنو إليَّ لأجازيك بأحسن ما أسديت إليَّ؟ هلمَّ إليَّ ولا تقطع إخائي، فإنه مَنْ اتخذ صديقًا وقطع إخاءه وأضاع صداقته حُرِمَ ثمرة إخائه وأيس من نفعه الإخوان والأصدقاء، وإن يدك عندي لا تنسى.
وأنت حقيق أن تلتمس مكافأة ذلك مني ومن إخواني وأصدقائي ولا تخاف مني شيئًا، واعلم أن ما قبلي لك مبذول، ثم حلف واجتهد على صديقه فيما قال.

فناداه الجرذ: رُبَّ صداقة ظاهرة باطنها عداوة كامنة وهي أشدُّ من العداوة الظاهرة، ومَنْ لم يحترس منها وقع موقع الرجل الذي يركب ناب الفيل الهائج ثم يغلبه النعاس فيستيقظ تحت فراسن الفيل فيدوسه ويقتله، وإنما سُمِّي الصديق صديقًا لما يُرجى من صدقه ونفعه، وسُمِّي العدوُّ عدوًا لما يُخافُ من اعتدائه وضرره، والعاقل إذا رجا نفع العدوِّ أظهر له الصداقة، وإذا خاف ضرَّ الصديق أظهر له العداوة. ألا ترى تتبع البهائم أماتها رجاء ألبانها فإذا انقطع ذلك انصرفت عنها؟ وربما قطع الصديق عن صديقه بعض ما كان يصله منه فلم يخف شرُّه لأن أصل أمره لم يكن عداوة، فأمَّا مَنْ كان أصل أمره عداوة جوهرية ثم أحدث صداقة لحاجة حملته على ذلك فإنه إذا زالت الحاجة التي حملته على ذلك زالت صداقته فتحوَّلت وصارت إلى أصل أمره، كالماء الذي يسخن بالنار فإذا رفع عنها عاد باردًا، وليس من أعدائي عدوُّ أضرُّ لي منك، وقد اضطرني وإياك حاجة إلى ما أحدثنا من المصالحة، وقد ذهب الأمر الذي احتجت إليَّ واحتجت إليك فيه، وأخاف أن يكون مع ذهابه عود العداوة.

ولا خير للضعيف في قرب العدوِّ القوي، ولا للذليل في قرب العدوِّ العزيز، ولا أعلم لك قبلي حاجة إلاَّ أن تكون تريد أكلي، ولا أعلم لي قبلك حاجة وليس عندي بك ثقة؛ فإني قد علمت أن الضعيف المحترس من العدو القوي أقرب إلى السلامة من القوي إذا اغترَّ بالضعيف واسترسل إليه. والعاقل يصالح عدوَّه إذا اضطر إليه ويصانعه ويظهر له ودَّه ويريه من نفسه الاسترسال إليه إذا لم يجد من ذلك بدًا، ثم يعجل الانصراف عنه حين يجد إلى ذلك سبيلاً.

واعلم أن سريع الاسترسال لا تقال عثرته، والعاقل يفي لمَنْ صالحه من أعدائه بما جعل له من نفسه ولا يثق به كل الثقة ولا يأمنه على نفسه مع القرب منه، وينبغي أن يبعد عنه ما استطاع، وأنا أودُّك من بعيد وأحبُّ لك من البقاء والسلامة ما لم أكن أحبُّه لك من قبل، وليس عليك أن تجازيني على صنيعي إلاَّ بمثل ذلك إذ لا سبيل إلى اجتماعنا، والسلام.

english.text: The Rat and the Cat

King Dabshalim said to Bidpai the philosopher, “I have heard this example. Give me an example of a man whose many enemies surround him on every side and bring him close to destruction. He seeks escape by making an alliance and peace with one of them, gains safety and freedom from fear, and then keeps faith with the enemy with whom he made peace.”

The philosopher said, “Friendship and enmity never remain forever in one condition. Friendship may turn into enmity, and enmity into alliance and friendship. Events, causes, and experiences bring this about. A person of judgment forms a new judgment for each new circumstance: strength in dealing with an enemy, familiarity in dealing with a friend. Past enmity should not prevent a sensible person from approaching an enemy and seeking his help to avert something feared or obtain something desired. Whoever acts prudently in this attains his purpose. An example is the rat and the cat, who fell into a predicament and both escaped their trouble and distress by making peace.”

“How was that?” asked the king.

Bidpai said, “They say that at the foot of a great tree was the den of a cat named Rumi. Nearby was the hole of a rat named Faridun. Hunters frequently visited that place to catch wild animals and birds. One day a hunter came and set his net near Rumi’s dwelling. Before long the cat was caught in it.

“The rat came creeping out, looking for food and wary of Rumi. As he searched, he saw the cat in the trap and rejoiced. Then he looked around and saw behind him a weasel ready to seize him, and in the tree an owl ready to snatch him away. He did not know what to do. If he went back, the weasel would take him; if right or left, the owl would snatch him; if forward, the cat would devour him.

“He thought, ‘Affliction has hemmed me in, evils have joined against me, and trials surround me. Yet my intelligence remains with me. I must not be frightened or overwhelmed by my situation, become bewildered, or let my heart scatter in panic. A sensible person with sound judgment does not lose courage or let his understanding desert him under any circumstances. Intelligence is like a sea whose depths cannot be reached. Adversity should not exhaust a person of judgment and destroy him; nor should the fulfillment of hope make him so exultant and intoxicated that his affairs become obscure to him. I see no escape from this trouble except peace with the cat. He has suffered a calamity like mine, or part of it. Perhaps if he listens to what I say, understands my clear words and my sincere truth, free of contradiction and deceit, and hopes for my assistance, we may both escape.’

“The rat approached the cat and asked, ‘How are you?’

“The cat said, ‘Just as you would wish: in hardship and confinement.’

“The rat said, ‘Today I share your trouble. I hope for no escape for myself except through what will also free you. There is no falsehood or deception in these words. The weasel is lying in wait for me, and the owl is watching me. Both are enemies to you and me. If you promise me safety, I will cut your bonds and release you from this predicament. Each of us will then be saved through the other, like a ship and its passengers at sea: they are saved by the ship, and the ship by them.’

“When the cat heard the rat and recognized his sincerity, he said, ‘Your words seem true. I too desire what I hope will save both you and me. If you do this, I will thank you for as long as I live.’

“The rat said, ‘I will come near and cut all the cords except one, which I will leave as security for myself against you.’ He began gnawing the bonds. When the owl and weasel saw the rat approach the cat, they despaired of catching him and went away.

“The rat took his time cutting Rumi’s bonds. The cat said, ‘Why do I not see you working earnestly to cut my cords? If you have obtained what you needed and changed your attitude, neglecting my need, that is not the conduct of good people. A noble person does not neglect his companion’s rights. You have seen the advantage and benefit of my earlier friendship. You ought to repay me for it and not remember the enmity between us. The peace we have made should make you forget it, along with the merit and reward of keeping faith and the evil consequences of treachery. A noble person is grateful, not resentful. One act of kindness makes him forget many injuries. It is said that the swiftest punishment is the punishment of treachery. Whoever, when implored and asked for forgiveness, shows neither mercy nor pardon has acted treacherously.’

“The rat said, ‘There are two kinds of friend: the willing friend and the friend compelled by necessity. Both seek benefit and guard against harm. One may freely trust the willing friend in all circumstances. With the compelled friend, one may be trusting in some circumstances and must be cautious in others. A sensible person always retains some hold upon the other’s needs against what he fears and guards against. The aim of such an association is immediate advantage and the attainment of one’s hope. I will fulfill my promise to you, while also guarding against you where I fear you, lest I suffer from you the very thing whose danger drove me to make peace and drove you to accept it. Every action has its proper time; performed at the wrong time, it has no good outcome. I will cut all your bonds, but leave one knot as a pledge. I will cut it only when I know that you are occupied with something other than me: when I see the hunter.’

“The rat continued cutting the cat’s cords. While he was doing so, the hunter arrived. The cat said, ‘Now is the time for earnest work at my bonds!’ The rat gnawed with all his might. When he finished, the cat sprang into the tree in alarm at the hunter, and the rat entered a crevice among the stones. The hunter came, picked up his cut net, and went away disappointed.

“Later the rat came out but did not wish to approach the cat. The cat called, ‘My sincere friend, who has rendered me such good service, what prevents you from coming near so I may repay your kindness with the best I can give? Come to me and do not break our brotherhood. Whoever acquires a friend, then breaks the bond and neglects the friendship, is deprived of its fruit and loses hope of benefit from brothers and friends. Your favor to me will not be forgotten. You ought to seek repayment from me and my brothers and friends. Fear nothing from me. Know that whatever I possess is at your disposal.’ He swore earnestly to the truth of his words.

“The rat called back, ‘Many an outward friendship conceals inward enmity, more dangerous than open hostility. Whoever does not guard against it is like a man riding on the tusk of a raging elephant who falls asleep and wakes beneath its feet, to be trampled to death. A friend is called a friend because of the benefit hoped for from him; an enemy is called an enemy because of the harm feared from him. When a sensible person hopes for benefit from an enemy, he shows him friendship; when he fears harm from a friend, he shows him hostility.

“‘Do you not see that young animals follow their mothers in hope of milk? When it ceases, they turn away. A friend may stop providing some benefit he formerly gave, yet the other need not fear harm from him, because the relationship did not begin in enmity. But one whose original condition was natural hostility, and who formed a friendship only because a need compelled him, loses that friendship when the need disappears. It turns back to hostility and returns to its original state, like water heated by fire, which becomes cold again when removed from it.

“‘None of my enemies is more harmful to me than you. Necessity compelled us both to make our peace. The circumstance in which you needed me and I needed you has passed, and I fear that its passing will restore our enmity.
